coredata.dc:description: Enzymatic degradation has been proposed as a suitable solution for addressing PET pollution, but approximately 10 % of PET is left as nonbiodegradable. Microbes can completely degrade PET at the gram level per year. Based on the complementary benefits of microbes and enzymes, a microbe-enzyme system was created to completely degrade PET. Here, a thermophilic microbe-enzyme (TME) system composed of Bacillus thermoamylovorans JQ3 and leaf-branch compost cutinase variant (ICCG) was used to demonstrate the synergistic degradation of PET, enabling 100 % degradation of PET waste at a high PET loading level (360 g/L). Six endogenous PET hydrolases of strain JQ3 were discovered by employing an ester bond hydrolysis function-first genome mining (EGM) strategy and first successfully expressed in E. coli. These hydrolases could release TPA as the final product from PET and preferentially degraded BHET instead of MHET. Of these, carboxylesterase 39_5 and ICCG could degrade PET in a synergistic manner to generate 50 μM of TPA, which was greater than the sum of the individual treatments. Finally, the degradation pathway of the TME system was speculated to include biofilm formation, PET degradation and utilization. The successful implementation of this study rendered a scale-up degradation feasible of PET at a lower cost.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Enzymatic degradation has been proposed as a suitable solution for addressing PET pollution, but approximately 10 % of PET is left as nonbiodegradable. Microbes can completely degrade PET at the gram level per year. Based on the complementary benefits of microbes and enzymes, a microbe-enzyme system was created to completely degrade PET. Here, a thermophilic microbe-enzyme (TME) system composed of Bacillus thermoamylovorans JQ3 and leaf-branch compost cutinase variant (ICCG) was used to demonstrate the synergistic degradation of PET, enabling 100 % degradation of PET waste at a high PET loading level (360 g/L). Six endogenous PET hydrolases of strain JQ3 were discovered by employing an ester bond hydrolysis function-first genome mining (EGM) strategy and first successfully expressed in E. coli. These hydrolases could release TPA as the final product from PET and preferentially degraded BHET instead of MHET. Of these, carboxylesterase 39_5 and ICCG could degrade PET in a synergistic manner to generate 50 μM of TPA, which was greater than the sum of the individual treatments. Finally, the degradation pathway of the TME system was speculated to include biofilm formation, PET degradation and utilization. The successful implementation of this study rendered a scale-up degradation feasible of PET at a lower cost.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Introduction
ce:section.ce:para: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), a widely used polyester-based plastic, is highly resistant to degradation and represents a serious ecological threat [1]. Landfilling and incineration are the two methods used to dispose of PET waste, and both can lead to the generation of toxic gases and secondary pollution [2]. Many efforts have been directed toward reducing PET waste, and the most promising and eco-friendly approach for the disposal of PET waste is biodegradation [3,4].

Over the last few years, a number of bacteria that are capable of degrading PET such as Ideonella sakaiensis [4], Stenotrophomonas pavanii [5], and Microbacterium oleivorans [6], have been discovered. However, the microbial degradation rate of PET is extremely slow at the gram level per year. Various PET hydrolases originating from microbes, including leaf-branch compost cutinase (LCC) [7], PETase [4], and Thermobifida fusca cutinase (TfCut) [8], have been identified. Considerable attention has been focused on enhancing PET hydrolysis. DuraPETase, a variant of PETase developed using a computational redesign (GRAPE) strategy, exhibited a 300-fold increase in the amount of product generated by PETase [9]. An LCC variant (ICCG) that degraded 90 % of PET at 200 g/L was created using a rational design approach [3].

Currently, enzymatic PET degradation using ICCG, the most typical representative with major breakthroughs, still has several limitations in its industrial application. Nearly 10 % of the total weight of PET is left as nonbiodegradable because of a marked increase in crystallinity [3]. Additionally, the expense of ICCG for PET degradation (3 kg protein/1 ton of PET) was roughly $225, including the costs of fermentation ($25 per kg of protein) and purification ($50 per kg of protein) associated with the cost of producing Trichoderma reesei cellulase [10]. Complete enzymatic degradation of PET at a low cost through process optimization presents a challenge, thus increasing the demand for a novel degradation system with balanced degradation efficiency and cost.

Microbe-enzyme systems are currently deemed highly efficient for PET degradation, as in the case of cellulose degradation [11]. A microbe-enzyme system comprising Microbacterium oleivorans and TfCut has been found to exhibit improved degradation performance in comparison to that of either microbe or enzyme treatment alone [6]. Huang et al. also reported the effectiveness of the Stenotrophomonas pavanii-TfCut system, which demonstrated microbe-enzyme synergy during PET degradation [5]. The hydrophobicity of PET was reduced by S. pavanii via colonization, which improved the adsorption of enzymes onto the surface of PET and thereby increased enzyme efficiency. Nonetheless, the ideal temperature for these systems is 30–40 °C, which is lower than the optimal temperature for PET degradation (60–75 °C) [12]. Hence, thermophilic microbe-enzyme (TME) systems are thought to be advantageous for PET degradation. PET hydrolases exhibit high-temperature resistance (Tm > 65 °C) [3]. Nevertheless, the absence of thermophilic PET-degrading bacteria impedes the development of an effective TME system.

In our previous study [13], five thermophilic PET-degrading bacteria, identified as Paenibacillus thermoaerophilus JQ1, Anoxybacillus rupiensis JQ2, Bacillus thermoamylovorans JQ3, Paenibacillus thermoaerophilus JQ4, and Anoxybacillus rupiensis JQ5, were isolated from a biofilm of PET waste in hot springs. The leaf-branch compost cutinase variant (ICCG) [3] was chosen as the enzyme for the TME system in this study, and an ideal thermophilic bacterium that acts in synergy with ICCG to degrade PET was screened. The TME system was then established and optimized to accomplish the scale-up degradation of PET waste at a lower cost. Potential endogenous PET hydrolases were discovered through an ester bond hydrolysis function-first genome mining (EGM) strategy. The resulting PET hydrolases were expressed and characterized in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells. Additionally, the PET degradation pathway within the TME system was also proposed to emphasize the significance of microbe-enzyme synergy.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Materials and methods
Chemicals, reagents, and bacterial sources
ce:section.ce:para: Amorphous PET (thickness 0.25 mm) was purchased from Goodfellow Ltd., UK. Terephthalic acid (TPA) and mono (2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai, China). Bis(hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) was obtained from Aladdin Industrial Co. (Shanghai, China). Other chemicals and solvents were supplied by Sinopec Group (Beijing, China). E. coli BL21(DE3) cells were obtained from our laboratory for the expression of recombinant enzymes. Thermophilic PET-degrading bacteria were isolated and deposited in our laboratory.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bacterial strain and cultivation
ce:section.ce:para: Stock cultures of PET-degrading bacteria were maintained as 50 % glycerol stocks at −80 °C. Five microliters of stock culture were inoculated into 100 mL of Luria-Bertani (LB) broth at the optimal temperature (Fig. S1) and incubated at 200 rpm overnight as a seed liquid (0.9 × 1010 CFU/mL) for further study.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression and purification of ICCG in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: The ICCG gene-encoding sequences were synthesized commercially and inserted between the NdeI and XhoI restriction enzyme sites of the expression plasmid pET20b. The recombinant plasmid pET20b-ICCG was transformed into E. coli through a standard protocol [14]. A single colony of recombinant E. coli was incubated as a seed culture in LB broth containing 100 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C and 200 rpm for 8 h. The 2 % (v/v) seed culture was added to 100 mL of LB broth supplemented with 100 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C and 200 rpm for 2 h, and then cultured for another 24 h with 0.4 mM IPTG induction at 25 °C. The supernatant was heated for 15 min at 70 °C and centrifuged for 30 min at 8000 r/min and 4 °C. The obtained supernatant containing the ICCG protein was stored at −80 °C until use in degradation experiments. The ICCG protein was verified by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) analysis [15], and the concentration was estimated by the Bradford method [16].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Evaluation of microbe-enzyme synergy for PET degradation
ce:section.ce:para: To obtain an optimal thermophilic bacterium that acts in synergy with ICCG to degrade PET, PET (120 mg) was incubated in 40 mL of M9 broth (6.78 g/L Na2HPO4, 3.0 g/L KH2PO4, 0.5 g/L NaCl, 1.0 g/L NH4Cl, 0.5 g/L MgSO4·7H2O, 0.1 g/L CaCl2, 4.0 g/L glucose) containing 1.8 × 108 CFU/mL microbe and 12.5 μg/mL ICCG at 60 °C with shaking at 200 rpm. Microbe and enzyme treatment alone were used as controls. Degradation effects were estimated based on various parameters, such as weight loss of PET, bacterial adhesion, and ICCG adsorption on PET surfaces.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation characteristics of the TME system on PET and oligomers
ce:section.ce:para: To investigate the degradation characteristics of the TME system composed of optimal PET-degrading bacteria and ICCG, PET degradation was carried out under the same conditions as those previously mentioned in Section 2.4. The weights of the residual PET and degradation products were determined every 12 h. The residual PET was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and Fourier transform-infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy. The degradation ability of the TME system on oligomers (BHET and MHET) was also evaluated. Briefly, 4 mg of oligomer was added to 10 mL of M9 broth and degraded using the TME system under the same conditions as those described above (Section 2.4). Microbe and enzyme treatment alone were used as controls as well as non-microbe and enzyme treatment. The residual weight of the oligomers was determined via HPLC analysis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Large-scale optimization of PET degradation
ce:section.ce:para: To improve the degradation efficiency of PET in the TME system, the effects of microbe concentration (0.3 × 108, 0.6 × 108, 1.2 × 108, 1.8 × 108, 2.4 × 108, 3.0 × 108, and 3.6 × 108 CFU/mL), enzyme dosage (6.25, 12.5, 25, 50, 75, and 100 μg/mL), reaction temperature (50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 72, and 75 °C), and reaction solution (mineral salt broth, normal saline, phosphate buffer, LB broth, and M9 broth) on PET degradation were investigated under the same conditions as those described above (Section 2.4). Following incubation, the optimal conditions were determined based on the weight loss of PET. On this basis, the PET loading level was further optimized (30, 60, 120, 240, 360, 480, and 600 g/L) using a 3-L Minibio bioreactor (New Brunswick BioFlo, Eppendorf). A single marine impeller was employed to maintain constant agitation at 200 rpm, while temperature regulation was accomplished through immersion in a water bath. During incubation, the residual weight of PET and degradation products was determined every 12 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Whole genome sequence and in silico analysis of endogenous PET hydrolases
ce:section.ce:para: The whole genome of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 was sequenced using the Illumina NovaSeq sequencing platform in GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China) and then deposited in GenBank. The EGM strategy was proposed to predict endogenous PET hydrolases by using a combination of gene annotation [17], phylogenetic analysis [18], KEGG and GO prediction [19], and molecular docking analysis [20].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Functional verification of endogenous PET hydrolases
Production and purification of endogenous PET hydrolases in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: The gene encoding sequences of the endogenous PET hydrolases were synthesized commercially and inserted between the NdeI and XhoI restriction enzyme sites of the expression plasmid pET24a. Recombinant E. coli were obtained and cultured using the same method used for ICCG (Section 2.4). After centrifugation for 30 min at 8000 r/min and 4 °C, the supernatant was subjected to ammonium sulfate precipitation (70 % w/v) and left to stand for 8–10 h. The precipitates were collected and dissolved in pH 8.0, 10 mM phosphate buffer for overnight dialysis. The fractions were collected and further purified using a nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) affinity column. The supernatant containing the endogenous PET hydrolases was characterized and stored at −80 °C until use in degradation experiments.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of pH and temperature on enzyme activity
ce:section.ce:para: Enzyme activity was determined using a previously described method [6] with p-nitrophenyl butyrate (p-NPB) as the substrate. The temperature optimum of the endogenous PET hydrolases was determined under temperatures ranging from 30 °C to 80 °C. The thermostability was determined at the optimal temperature, and residual activity was measured using the p-NPB method. Enzyme activity in buffers of various pH values (4.0–8.0) was measured. The buffers were as follows (20 mM): sodium acetate (pH 4.0–5.5), sodium phosphate (pH 6.0–7.5), Tris-HCl (pH 8.0–9.0), and glycine-NaOH (pH 9.5–10.0). The pH stability was examined at the optimal pH and temperature, and the residual activity was measured in the manner previously mentioned.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity of endogenous PET hydrolases
ce:section.ce:para: To determine the substrate specificity of the endogenous PET hydrolases, 4 mg of oligomer was added to 10 mL of 50 mM Tris-HCl, and the mixture was then incubated at 60 °C and 120 rpm with a final concentration of endogenous PET hydrolases at 1 mg/mL. During incubation, the supernatant was obtained by centrifugation and analyzed by HPLC.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Synergistic degradation of endogenous PET hydrolase and ICCG on PET
ce:section.ce:para: To investigate the synergistic effect of endogenous PET hydrolase and ICCG on PET degradation, 120 mg of PET was incubated in 40 mL of pH 8.0 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer at 60 °C and 120 rpm with a final concentration of endogenous PET hydrolase at 12.5 μg/mL plus ICCG at 12.5 μg/mL. As a control, PET was performed by using the ICCG alone. After incubating for 96 h, the supernatant was obtained by centrifugation and subjected to HPLC analysis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Analytical methods
Characterization of residual PET
ce:section.ce:para: The residual PET was washed sequentially using 2 % (w/v) SDS and absolute alcohol. After air drying, the weight loss of PET was determined as the weight difference between the initial and residual PET [21]. The surface morphology of the residual PET was observed using SEM. The chemical changes in the surficial structure of residual PET were analyzed using a Spectrum 400 FT-IR in the frequency range of 4000–400 cm−1 with 4 cm−1 resolution and 10 scanning mode.

ce:section.ce:section-title: HPLC analysis of degradation products
ce:section.ce:para: Degradation products released from PET degradation were determined using an Agilent 1100 model HPLC equipped with an Ultimate XB-C18 column (4.6 × 250 mm, 5 μm, Welch). The mobile phase was methanol with 1 % (w/v) aqueous acetic acid at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min, and detection was performed using a UV detector at 254 nm. The product yield was calculated based on the corresponding standard curves.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Statistical analysis
ce:section.ce:para: All tests were performed in triplicate, and the data are presented as the mean and standard deviation. The statistical significance was determined at the 5 % level using GraphPad Prism software.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Results and discussion
Evaluation of microbe-enzyme synergy in PET degradation
ce:section.ce:para: Successful expression of ICCG (28 kDa) was achieved in E. coli, followed by extracellular secretion with the help of the signal peptide PelB (Fig. 1A). Signal peptides are short peptides that carry information for protein secretion and are located in the N-terminus of the protein in the recombinant plasmid pET20b [23]. After heat treatment, the ICCG activity increased from 5.9 U/mL to 76.75 U/mL. This increase was attributed to the ability of heat treatment to denature and precipitate almost proteins from the host, improving the purity of the ICCG protein. A similar observation was made with Thermobifida fusca cutinase [24].

Among these bacteria, B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 in combination with ICCG significantly enhanced the degradation of PET (Fig. 1B). After 48 h, the weight loss of PET reached 65.1 %, which was greater than the sum of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 (0.5 %) and ICCG (3.6 %) treatment alone. SEM revealed that B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 exhibited a higher capacity for biofilm formation than the other organisms (Fig. 1C). Previous studies reported that biofilm formation could improve the adsorption of enzymes on the PET surface by reducing the hydrophobicity of PET [5,25]. The degree of ICCG adsorption on the PET surface initially increased at first and subsequently decreased over time (Fig. 1D). The AD of ICCG in the B. thermoamylovorans JQ3-ICCG system was 70 % after 60 h of incubation, which was higher than the AD of the other combinations. These findings implied that B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 could promote the immobilization of more ICCG on the PET surface through biofilm formation, which enhanced the degradation activity at 60 °C. From an evolutionary standpoint, adherent microbes are beneficial for the degradation of insoluble substrates (e.g., cellulose) by increasing the amount of the enzyme that degrades the substrate (more enzyme on the substrate surface and/or less enzyme in the supernatant) [26]. It is believed that the hydrolysis of cellulose by microbes is also accompanied by biofilm formation [27]. Thus, the TME system consisting of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 and ICCG showed the potential to synergistically degrade PET.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation characteristics of the TME system on PET and oligomers
ce:section.ce:para: The time-course curve of PET degradation and TPA accumulation showed a linear relationship over the first 36 h in the TME system, and then a subsequent linear decay rate was observed (Fig. 2A). The TME system exhibited significant PET degradation (e.g., ubiquitous cracks on the surface), with nearly 100 % of the PET degraded within 84 h (e.g., PET degraded into small pieces) (Fig. 2B). The highest degradation rate was observed between 24 and 36 h at approximately 3.0 mg PET h−1, with the maximum productivity of TPA at 2.7 mg h−1. However, the highest DS value (∼15.8) was observed after 48 h. DS values >2 are common [6], and DS values >5 have been reported [28]. Analysis of the FT-IR spectra showed that each peak appeared to gradually decreased over time, and the pattern was similar for the initial and residual PET (Fig. 2C). As shown in Fig. 2D and E, the TME system was able to degrade BHET and MHET, which exhibited similar degradation rates upon ICCG treatment alone, indicating that there was no microbe-enzyme synergy in the degradation of PET oligomers. This phenomenon was in contradiction to the results obtained from the Microbacterium oleivorans-cutinase system [6]. The TME system was successfully proposed based on microbe-enzyme synergy and was specifically tailored for PET degradation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: PET degradation in the TME system on a large scale
ce:section.ce:para: At the shake flask level, various parameters affecting PET degradation were optimized through 48 h of incubation at 60 °C and 200 rpm (Fig. 3A). The weight loss of PET increased and then decreased with increasing microbe concentration, peaking at 62.7 % with 1.8–2.4 × 108 CFU/mL (Fig. 3B). Variations in enzyme dosage resulted in fluctuations of PET degradation (Fig. 3C). Low enzyme dosages (6.25–12.5 μg/mL) exhibited a greater degradation effect than high enzyme dosages. A similar hydrolytic phenomenon was observed for PETase [29], as a low dosage of 0.5 mg of enzyme/g PET resulted in approximately 2-fold greater degradation than a higher dosage (3 mg of enzyme/g PET). As the inner core of PET is only minimally permeated by the enzyme as a result of typical surface erosion processes, only a limited number of superficial ester bonds are accessible to the enzyme, even when present in great excess [30]. As shown in Fig. 3D, no discernable variation in PET degradation was observed at 50–75 °C (62.7 %–64.5 %). Tournier et al. demonstrated that high temperature accelerated PET recrystallization, which is detrimental to PET degradation [3]. The reaction solution had a major impact on PET degradation (Fig. 3E). Mineral salt broth showed the highest level of PET degradation, at 98.3 %. According to previous reports, gly-OH buffer enhances the degradation activity of PETase and thus represents an optimal reaction solution [4].

The scale-up degradation of PET at 30, 60, 120, 240, 360, 400, and 600 g/L is shown in Fig. 4A. Nearly complete degradation of PET was achieved in 96 h at PET loading levels of 30–360 g/L in mineral salt broth at 1.8 × 108 CFU/mL microbes and 6.25 μg/mL enzyme at 60 °C (Fig. 4B-F). At 480 and 600 g/L PET, the maximum degree of PET degradation was observed, ranging from 62.3 %–64.2 % (Fig. 4G-H), which was in line with the findings of a previous report [31], indicating that the substrate inhibition might occur at high substrate concentrations. The complete degradation of PET at 360 g/L demonstrated the feasibility of large-scale degradation of PET. In the TME system, the generation rate of TPA (2.7 g/L h−1) was lower than that of ICCG (42.9 g TPA/L h−1) [3] and TurboPETase (77.3 g TPA/L h−1) [30] as a result of microbes using of TPA as a carbon source [4]. Previous studies have indicated that enzyme consumption is likely to be greater than that required at optimal pH because of the untimely regulation of the reaction pH (pH 8) using NaOH solution, which leads to the inactivation of enzymes in acidic environments [3,32]. However, the pH of the TME system was not adjusted during operation. The biofilm of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 on the PET surface provided a stable microenvironment that enhanced the pH tolerance of ICCG (Fig. S2). Moreover, the amount of ICCG consumed in the TME system is 17.3 g per ton of PET ($1.34), approximately 0.8 % of the amount used with ICCG treatment alone (3 kg per ton of PET, $225) [3] and 1.05 % of the amount used with TurboPETase (2 kg per ton of PET, $150) [30]. The production cost of Trichoderma reesei was used to estimate the total cost of the microbes [10], which was $5 per liter of seed liquid (10 mL of seed liquid per ton of PET, $0.05). These results proved that the TME system could completely degrade PET waste at a much lower cost and on a large industrial scale.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Whole genome sequence and in silico analysis of endogenous PET hydrolases
ce:section.ce:para: Whole-genome sequencing is a useful method for discovering novel PET hydrolases [4]. The whole genome sequence of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 was completed (GenBank SRR18149614) and characterized, as shown in Table S1. The EGM strategy was proposed (Fig. 5A) and used to identify 126 genes encoding endogenous hydrolases. Of these, forty-five hydrolases, such as lipases, esterases, cutinases, and carboxylesterases, were identified as ester bond hydrolases. Homology alignment of the genes with reference genes in databases (e.g., KEGG and GO) indicated that these enzymes might be involved in PET degradation (Table S2). The gene-deduced amino acid sequences were compared with those of known PET hydrolases (e.g., PETase and LCC) using phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 5B). The six gene-deduced amino acid sequences that clustered with known PET hydrolases were chosen and annotated as a lipase (Lip4_120), esterases (Est8_89, Est11_32, and Est18_23), and carboxylesterases (Ces19_14 and Ces39_5). Molecular docking analysis demonstrated that the above endogenous hydrolases could accommodate 2HE-(MHET)5 (Fig. 5C). A characteristic cap domain was observed in Lip4_120, Est8_89, Ces19_14, and Ces39_5, which might inhibit the entry of macromolecular substrates into the binding groove, as in the case of the lipase EstA [33]. In contrast, the catalytic centers of Ces39_5, Est11_32, and Est18_23 were visible on the surface of the enzyme without a characteristic cap. Interestingly, the catalytic center of Ces39_5 had a large available space on the side of the catalytic residue, which was favorable for binding macromolecular substrates (e.g., PET).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Functional verification of endogenous PET hydrolases
Expression and purification of endogenous PET hydrolases in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: To investigate its functionality, six endogenous PET hydrolases were intracellular expressed in E. coli BL21. SDS-PAGE analysis revealed possible homogeneous bands with molecular weights of 43.3 kDa (Lip4_120), 30.3 kDa (Est8_89), 29.8 kDa (Est11_32), 54.9 kDa (Est18_23), 27.8 kDa (Ces19_14), and 28.6 kDa (Ces39_5), which coincided with the predicted weights (Fig. 6A). The following activities of Lip4_120, Est8_89, Est11_32, Est18_23, Ces19_14, and Ces39_5 reached 1738.6 U/mL, 11.2 U/mL, 5.6 U/mL, 95.4 U/mL, 5.7 U/mL, and 10.4 U/mL, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of temperature and pH on endogenous PET hydrolases
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 6B showed that each endogenous PET hydrolase was active at 30–80 °C, with optimal activity at 40 °C for Lip4_120, Est11_32, and Ces19_14 and at 50 °C for Est8_89, Est18_23, and Ces39_5. Notably, these activities decreased sharply from 60 °C to 80 °C (Fig. 6C). These endogenous PET hydrolases exhibited a low degree of thermostability at the optimal temperature. Of these, Est11_32 exhibited greater thermostability, maintaining over 60.0 % of the maximal activity after incubating at 60 °C for 30 min, and its half-life was 40 min. The optimal pH for the activity of these endogenous PET hydrolases was pH 7.0, and the relative activity at the pH 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0 was over 50.0 % of maximal activity (Fig. 6D). As shown in Fig. 6E, the activity of these endogenous PET hydrolases exceeded over 60.0 % of the maximal activity after incubation at pH 8.0 for 1 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Specificity of endogenous PET hydrolases on the MHET and BHET
ce:section.ce:para: As shown in Fig. 6F, these endogenous PET hydrolases could degrade 90 % of the MHET in 36 h with no discernible variation. By comparison, there was a significant difference in the degradation effects of endogenous PET hydrolases on BHET (Fig. 6G). Lip4_120, Est18_23, and Ces39_5 had higher degradation potentials than the other strains, with approximately 100 % degradation of BHET in 1 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Synergistic degradation of endogenous PET hydrolase and ICCG on PET
ce:section.ce:para: TPA was detected as the final product in PET hydrolase-treated PET solution after 4 h of incubation (Fig. 6H). The highest accumulation of TPA was observed with Ces19_14 (3.4 μM), followed by Lip4_120 (2.4 μM) and Ces39_5 (1.9 μM). However, the highest binding free energy of 2-HE(MHET)5 was observed with Ces39_5 (−4.62 ± 0.23 kcal/mol), followed by Ces19_14 (−4.23 ± 0.23 kcal/mol) and Lip4_120 (−3.85 ± 0.15 kcal/mol). The results of the binding free energy and degradation experiments differed because the molecular docking analysis was performed under simulation of a vacuum environment, which lacks desolvation energy and PET bioavailability [34]. The accumulation of TPA was detected in experiments in which the above PET hydrolases were combined with ICCG (Fig. 6I). The highest accumulation of TPA as a final product (53 μM) was detected with the combined use of Ces39_5 and ICCG at 4 h, and this accumulation was greater than the sum of individual enzyme treatments (1.9 μM for Ces39_5, and 15 μM for ICCG). Various multi-enzyme systems, such as a dual enzyme system composed of LCC and TfCut, have been proposed as optimal choices for PET degradation [35].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Analysis of the degradation pathway in the TME system
ce:section.ce:para: The PET degradation pathway of the TME system involves three potential steps: 1) biofilm formation, 2) PET degradation, and 3) PET utilization (Fig. 7 ). Initially, a biofilm was formed by B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 on the PET surface, which facilitated the immobilization of additional more PET hydrolase (e.g., ICCG) on the PET surface and provided a stable microenvironment for the microbes and the enzyme (e.g., enhanced pH tolerance). The significant up-regulation of genes related to biofilm formation, such as genes associated with quorum sensing, flagellar assembly, and bacterial chemotaxis, was detected in line with the results of the experiments (Fig. S3 and Table S3). Furthermore, there was an increase in the expression of PET hydrolase-associated genes, which produced additional enzymes for subsequent degradation. As a result of microbe-enzyme synergy, ubiquitous cracks appeared on the PET surface, and soluble TPA was released as a product from PET. Ultimately, these soluble products, as carbon sources, are taken up as carbon sources by the microbes and metabolized via the tricarboxylic acid cycle to support growth. The newly generated microbes then initiate PET degradation, repeating the above steps.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Conclusion
ce:section.ce:para: In summary, a novel TME system consisting of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 and ICCG was developed to achieve 100 % degradation of PET waste at 360 g/L PET. This system significantly outperformed previous technologies for large-scale PET degradation due to its lower cost and no requirement for pH adjustment. A total of six endogenous PET hydrolases of B. thermoamylovorans JQ3 were discovered using the EGM strategy. These hydrolases were expressed in E. coli and exhibited the degradation ability of PET. This study describes the development of a highly efficient, stable, and controllable microbe-enzyme system for the large-scale degradation of PET waste.
